subject: European History
title: 4. The Eastern Question, Crimean War and Russo-Turkish War

segments.text: “Eastern Question” should always trigger the same three-part framework: Ottoman decline, Balkan nationalism, and rivalry among Russia, Austria-Hungary, Britain and other powers — never reduce it to a single war.

The Ottoman Empire’s weakening control over parts of Europe, combined with reform efforts that struggled to keep pace with external pressure, encouraged neighbouring powers to compete over the fate of Ottoman lands. Greek, Serbian, Bulgarian, Romanian and other nationalist movements developed with different specific goals, frequently seeking outside-power support and thereby internationalising what began as local rebellions. Russia presented itself partly as protector of Orthodox Christians while pursuing strategic influence around the Black Sea and the Straits, a combination other powers feared would upset the wider European balance.

The great-power revision of San Stefano, reshaping the Balkans and setting up later tensions.
Use a map of the Balkans and Black Sea; prepare “Ottoman weakness + nationalism + great-power rivalry” as the three constant forces, then place each war and treaty into that framework.
Practise one analytical outline answering: “Why did the great powers revise the Treaty of San Stefano at the Congress of Berlin?”
Do not define the Eastern Question as simply “the Crimean War”; it lasted for decades.
Do not ignore Balkan nationalism when discussing great-power rivalry.
Do not confuse San Stefano with Berlin; Berlin revised the earlier Russian-imposed settlement.
The Crimean War was fought from 1853 to 1856; Britain and France joined the Ottoman Empire against Russia.
The Treaty of Paris (1856) temporarily limited Russian influence in the Black Sea region.
Russia defeated the Ottoman Empire in the war of 1877–78.
The Treaty of San Stefano was revised at the Congress of Berlin in 1878 because other powers feared excessive Russian influence.

The Eastern Question is a decades-long structural problem, not a single event, and every sub-episode should be explained through the same three-part framework (Ottoman decline, Balkan nationalism, great-power rivalry).
Austria-Hungary’s 1878 occupation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, agreed at Berlin, is a direct causal thread running forward into the origins of the First World War.
